arcs.title: Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem (1986–1995)
arcs.description: Andrew Wiles spent seven years constructing a proof that no positive integers a, b, c satisfy a^n + b^n = c^n for n > 2. The proof did not attack the equation directly. Wiles instead established a special case of the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture: every semistable elliptic curve over the rationals is modular. Combined with Frey's curve construction and Ribet's level-lowering theorem, this implies FLT. Wiles built his proof through deformation theory of Galois representations, an R = T isomorphism between deformation rings and Hecke algebras, and a passage from residual modularity (mod 3, mod 5) to full modularity. The first announcement (1993) had a gap in the Euler system step; Wiles and Richard Taylor closed it (1995) by replacing the failed Euler system argument with a different technique using Iwasawa theory.

arcs.title: Alexander Grothendieck's introduction of schemes (1957–1970)
arcs.description: Algebraic geometry before Grothendieck studied varieties: solution sets of polynomial equations over fields. Grothendieck replaced the variety with the SCHEME, an object built from any commutative ring's prime spectrum, glued along a sheaf of rings. This let Grothendieck handle: nilpotent elements (which varieties cannot see), arithmetic and geometry simultaneously (number rings and function fields became the same kind of object), generic points, base changes, families of varieties parametrized by another scheme. He developed étale cohomology to give Weil-style cohomology theories with coefficients in finite fields, eventually leading to Deligne's proof of the Weil conjectures. The construction proceeded by identifying universal properties (every construction had to be characterized by what mapped into or out of it) and by demanding that all definitions be functorial.

arcs.title: Jacob Lurie's Higher Topos Theory and ∞-categories (2009)
arcs.description: Mathematicians had several models of weak higher categories that were equivalent in spirit but technically incompatible. Lurie selected the quasicategory model (Joyal/Boardman-Vogt) and built a comprehensive theory: an infinity-categorical version of category theory that includes adjoint functors, limits, colimits, Kan extensions, and a full theory of ∞-topoi. The motivation was that derived categories, stable homotopy theory, and étale homotopy types had been suffering from the lack of a categorical framework that handled them natively. By promoting homotopy-coherent versions of every standard categorical construction, Lurie made it possible to do derived algebraic geometry, derived deformation theory, and topological field theory inside a single language.

arcs.title: Peter Scholze's perfectoid spaces and diamonds (2011–present)
arcs.description: Scholze defined a perfectoid space: a topological ring object satisfying a Frobenius lift condition that lets characteristic-0 and characteristic-p geometry be tilted into each other. Scholze used perfectoid spaces to give a uniform proof of Deligne's weight-monodromy conjecture in many cases, prove the local Langlands correspondence in new settings, and build new cohomology theories. He later introduced diamonds, which are quotients of perfectoid spaces by pro-étale equivalence relations, and used them to define the Fargues-Fontaine curve in a way that unified p-adic Hodge theory with global Langlands. Each step was motivated by a specific gap: a phenomenon was visible empirically (e.g., the Frobenius-perfection trick in p-adic Hodge theory) but lacked a unified object that made it categorical.

arcs.title: Riemann's introduction of Riemann surfaces (1851–1857)
arcs.description: Bernhard Riemann was confronted with multi-valued analytic functions like sqrt(z) and log(z), which mathematicians of his time had handled by branch cuts and conventions about which value to pick. Riemann replaced the multi-valued function on the complex plane with a single-valued function on a new geometric object — the Riemann surface — constructed by gluing copies of the plane together along the branch cuts. This transformed the study of algebraic functions into the study of compact orientable two-manifolds equipped with complex structure, whose topology (genus, cycles) carried structural information about the function. The Riemann-Roch theorem then connected the topological invariants of the surface to dimensions of spaces of meromorphic functions and differentials on it.

arcs.title: Newton's invention of calculus and the principia (1665–1687)
arcs.description: Newton confronted simultaneous problems: tangent lines to curves, instantaneous velocities, areas under curves, and planetary orbits. Existing methods handled each in isolation. Newton introduced fluxions (derivatives) and the inverse method (integrals) and recognized them as inverse operations. He developed the calculus of infinite series for handling functions defined implicitly. He treated instantaneous velocity as a limit of average velocities — a concept that took two centuries to be made rigorous. Applied to physics: gravity acts at a distance, the same law (inverse-square) explains both falling apples and elliptical planetary orbits, and a small set of axioms (three laws of motion, universal gravitation) yields all of celestial mechanics. Calculus and physics co-evolved: each was needed to make the other operational.

arcs.title: Einstein's General Relativity (1907–1915)
arcs.description: Einstein began with the equivalence principle: a uniformly accelerating frame is indistinguishable from a uniform gravitational field. Over eight years he searched for a tensor-valued field equation that recovered Newtonian gravity in the weak-field limit, was generally covariant (no preferred frames), and conserved energy-momentum. Mathematical inputs from Marcel Grossmann and the Ricci-Levi-Civita absolute differential calculus (now called tensor calculus) provided the language. Einstein's 1913 'Entwurf' theory failed (not generally covariant). The 1915 field equations G_μν = 8πG T_μν resulted from realizing that the Bianchi identities forced the form of the equation once general covariance was demanded. Two predictions were specific and falsifiable: perihelion of Mercury (43 arcsec/century, observed match within one year) and bending of starlight (Eddington 1919 confirmed it).

arcs.title: Polya's How to Solve It (1945) and Hadamard's Psychology of Invention (1945)
arcs.description: Polya systematized the heuristics of mathematical problem-solving: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back. Inside the 'devise a plan' step Polya catalogued moves: have you seen this before? specialize, generalize, consider an analogous problem, work backward, decompose, recombine, vary the problem (drop a hypothesis, weaken a conclusion, swap roles of given and unknown). Hadamard documented his and others' (notably Poincaré's) introspective accounts of discovery: a period of conscious work, then incubation, then sudden insight, then verification. Both works refused to claim mechanical algorithms — heuristics are guides, not procedures, and the moment of insight resists decomposition.
